newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS-NATO INVITE SEEN HAVING LITTLE EFFECT ON HUNGARY SHRS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NATO INVITE SEEN HAVING LITTLE EFFECT ON HUNGARY SHRS.

text.p: NATO's invitation to Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic to join the alliance will have little impact on Hungarian stock prices as the move was widely expected, analysts said on Tuesday.
"(There's) probably not a lot of impact in overall terms," said Nigel Rendell, Emerging European Strategist at HSBC James Capel in London.
"(But) this is the confirmation that the countries reached the stage of political and economic development which seems consistent with what the West would like," Rendell said.
A NATO summit in Madrid on Tuesday agreed to invite Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic to join the alliance and named Romania and Slovenia as deserving cases when enlargement is reviewed in 1999.
Another London-based analyst also saw the move as essentially confirming the three central European states' successful reforms.

"It's largely symbolic, but clearly it does underline how advanced Hungary is in its transition process, not simply in the economy, but what's happening to democracy," said Anthony Thomas, Director at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

Market participants said recently that beside the economic recovery and strong corporate earnings, the expected invitation was one reason behind the continuous strengthening and successive record highs on the Budapest Stock Exchange.
On Tuesday the BUX index finished at a fifth successive closing high of 7,241.09 points, up 43.27.
The analysts said that since the invitation was expected it could not catch market participants unawares. The opposite would be the real surprise, they added.

"It won't come as a surprise to the market, I think it is pretty well in the price at the moment," Dresdner Kleinwort Benson's Thomas said. "The real surprise would be if...Hungary were not invited to join NATO."
A third analyst also believed the NATO factor was mostly priced in by foreign investors and thus perhaps only local investors would react.
"Hungarian buyers might see this as an extra positive, but I really think that from foreign prospective it's fully discounted," said Frances Cloud, analyst at Nomura Equity Research.
